controls.label: Shape
controls.qualification: A sphere of the published radius, lit by TRAPPIST-1; the neutral gray is a display convention, not a measured color.
controls.notes: No image or color of TRAPPIST-1e exists: it is known from the dips it makes in its star's light and from the way the seven planets pull on each other. The gray marks an unresolved surface; the lighting is TRAPPIST-1's, at the measured orbit. The gray takes the color of trappist-1's light, as its color dataset measures it.

controls.label: Illustration
controls.qualification: NASA's artist's concept of TRAPPIST-1e, from Eyes on Exoplanets; not an observation.
controls.notes: NASA's artist's concept of TRAPPIST-1e: the map its Eyes on Exoplanets app wraps around the planet. Nobody has resolved this planet's disc, so none of the color, clouds or terrain in it was observed. Its longitudes are arbitrary.

controls.label: Climate model
controls.qualification: Simulation · ExoCAM · Wolf et al. (2022) · False color
controls.notes: Surface temperature of TRAPPIST-1e in the ExoCAM simulation of Wolf et al. (2022): a model, not a measurement. The run assumes one bar of nitrogen with 400 ppm of carbon dioxide over a global ocean, the THAI "Hab 1" case, on a planet that keeps one face to its star. The map is the mean state the release holds. Nobody has detected an atmosphere on TRAPPIST-1e. JWST's first transit spectra give no strong evidence for or against one: a nitrogen-rich atmosphere fits them, and so does bare rock (Glidden et al. 2025). Four models ran this case for the THAI comparison, and their global mean surface temperatures differ by 14 K (Sergeev et al. 2022). The false color runs from 200 to 300 K; it is not what an eye would see. With shadows on, the star's light darkens the night half.
